question: The Commission has proposed creating the European Competitiveness Fund as one of the key instruments of the next multiannual financial framework, which aims to boost the competitiveness of the EU economy in the areas of digital transformation, green transition, health and defence.

This proposal fits into the broader logic of creating further funds to offset the regulatory and investment costs of the Commission’s climate policy, which, in many sectors, weakens the competitiveness of EU industry rather than strengthening it.

The European Court of Auditors pointed out that the proposal is based on imprecise definitions of key concepts, in particular the EU’s added value and strategic dependencies, and on a performance-based funding model without independent verification of actual costs.

In the Court’s view, this makes it difficult to assess the effectiveness of the fund, control spending and clearly distinguish between interventions funded by the European Competitiveness Fund and those funded by other EU instruments. In light of the above: 1.

What specific and measurable criteria does the Commission intend to adopt in order to define the EU’s added value and assess the real impact of the European Competitiveness Fund on the competitiveness of the EU economy?
How will the Commission ensure independent and reliable verification of the use of funds in a performance-based model, to make it possible to determine what these funds were actually used for?
What coordination and control mechanisms does the Commission envisage to avoid overlaps between interventions funded by the European Competitiveness Fund and those funded by other EU instruments?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.

2026) As per the Commission’s Better Regulation framework, EU added value is considered from two perspectives: a forward-looking dimension (before the regulation proposals), reflected in impact assessments accompanying regulation proposals, and a backward-looking dimension (analysing past implementation and lesson learnt), which is carried out through annual performance monitoring and in the evaluations.

Annual performance monitoring will be conducted through the Performance Regulation1 framework, which relies on a common set of intervention fields for expenditure monitoring and on harmonised output and result indicators for performance measurement. In addition, EU added value is a key criterion in the evaluations, which allow for a more comprehensive and in-depth assessment of the programmes.

The Commission has proposed streamlining the EU budget to minimise overlaps and maximise synergies, reducing administrative burdens for Member States and others. Shared management and directly managed programmes (e.g.

the European Competitiveness Fund2 (ECF) and the Connecting Europe Facility3) include provisions for cumulative funding, allowing a single legal commitment and unified rules for actions funded by two programmes. This aims to simplify procedures, reduce audit risk, and improve efficiency and coherence. Specific coordination mechanisms in the ECF Regulation will enhance connections with complementary programmes.

A new steering mechanism will strengthen ties between policy coordination and the EU budget, fostering discussions about key financing priorities and enhancing budget flexibility to address evolving EU priorities.
